h1: Passing a food safety audit in a brewpub kitchen
title: Passing a Brewpub Food Safety Audit | Craft Beer School
desc: How a brewpub kitchen prepares for a food safety audit: licence, temperature logs, cross contamination, cleaning records, pest control and staff checks.
teaser: Auditors rarely fail a kitchen for bad food. They fail it for missing records. Here is what to have on the wall and in the folder.
standfirst: A brewpub kitchen shares a roof with a brewhouse. That means wet floors, spent grain, drains and steam sit near the food. A food safety audit checks that the two worlds stay apart and that you can prove it on paper.
sections: What an audit really looks for

An auditor walks the kitchen, reads the records and asks staff questions. They look at three things. Can the premises keep food safe? Does the team know how? Can you show it day after day? A kitchen that is clean on the audit day but has no records for the last three months usually loses points.

The auditor may come from the food regulator, from a hotel group or landlord that sets its own standards, or from a certification body you hired. In India the national food regulator is FSSAI. Rules, formats and inspection practice change, so check what applies to your premises with your licensing adviser or a food safety consultant. This guide covers habits that every auditor expects.
Licences and paperwork on the wall

Start with the basics. Your food business licence or registration should be valid and displayed where the rules require. Keep copies of the water test report, pest control contract, staff medical fitness records, training certificates and supplier details in one folder that anyone can find. If the manager is away, the second in command should know where it is.

For a brewpub, keep the alcohol licence conditions in the same office. A food audit and a licence inspection are different exercises, but an inspector who sees disorder in one will look harder at the other.

Temperature control is the heart of kitchen safety. Commonly used guidance keeps chilled food at or below about 5 °C, frozen food at about minus 18 °C and hot food above about 60 °C until served. Check your local requirement and write your own limits on the log sheet.

Fit a thermometer in every fridge and freezer. Record the reading at least at opening and closing, with initials. Use a probe thermometer to check cooked food. Clean the probe between uses. Calibrate probes on a schedule: a simple check in ice water should read about 0 °C. A log full of identical numbers with no corrections looks invented, so record real readings and what you did when one was out of range.

Cross contamination is a common reason for a failed audit. Use separate boards, knives and containers for raw meat, vegetables and ready to eat food, with colour coding that staff understand. Store raw meat below cooked food in the fridge so drips cannot fall onto it. Label every container with the product and the date it was prepared or opened. Use a first in, first out rule. Throw out anything past its date, not the day after.

Wash hands at dedicated hand wash basins with soap and a way to dry them, not at the pot sink. Check that every basin has both, every shift.
Where the brewhouse meets the kitchen

This is what is special about a brewpub. A brewhouse produces steam, wet floors, hot water, spent grain and cleaning chemicals. Keep them out of the food area. Spent grain should leave by a route that does not cross the kitchen. Store caustic and acid in labelled containers away from food and away from open drains that lead into the kitchen. Check that floor drains from the brewery do not back up into the cooking area.

Our guide on brewpub layout explains why the design decides how easy this is. An audit is far easier to pass if the layout already separates the two functions.

Every area needs a written cleaning schedule showing what is cleaned, how often, with what product and by whom. Staff should sign when done. Hoods and exhaust filters, grease traps, floor drains and the underside of equipment are often missed.

Hire a licensed pest control service and keep their visit reports. Seal gaps under doors, fit screens on windows and keep bins covered. Remove waste from the kitchen several times a day. Brewery waste, such as spent yeast, needs its own bin so it does not attract flies into food areas.
Train the team and rehearse the day

Auditors talk to staff. Ask your cooks the questions an auditor would: what temperature should this fridge be, how do you wash your hands, what do you do if you are ill. Teach everyone to answer plainly and honestly. A cook who says 'I would tell my manager and not handle food' scores better than one who bluffs.

Do a mock audit one week before the real one. Walk the kitchen with the checklist, fix what you find and write down what you fixed. Our guide on starting a beer and food delivery kitchen covers extra points if your kitchen also produces for delivery. Read brewpub food menu and margins too, because shortcuts on food cost are where hygiene often slips.

Running both a kitchen and a brewery well is a management problem before it is a technical one. Brewery Business Management teaches the planning that keeps standards up when the pub is full.
faqs: What do food safety auditors check first?
Usually the licence, cleanliness and the records. They then look at temperatures, storage, cross contamination and staff hygiene.
What temperatures should a kitchen record?
Fridges, freezers and cooked or hot held food. Commonly used limits are about 5 °C or lower for chilled, about minus 18 °C for frozen and above about 60 °C for hot holding.
Does a brewpub kitchen need anything extra?
Yes. Keep brewery steam, spent grain, chemicals and drains away from the food area and show that you do.
How soon before an audit should I do a mock audit?
About a week. It leaves time to fix what you find and to update records.
